title: Seedless bootstrap factory pattern — bare metal + vSphere playbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a working playbook for a 'seedless' cluster bootstrap factory pattern that can handle mixed bare-metal and vSphere fleets. It's intentionally procedural and experimental — the goal is a repeatable, idempotent bootstrap flow that minimizes stateful seed nodes and accelerates cluster reprovisioning for Private deployments.

Status and scope:
- Draft: exploratory runbook + Terraform module implementation notes.
- Target environments: on-prem bare metal racks with PXE/IPXE + BMC, and vSphere vCenter-based provisioning in the same management plane.
- Not in scope: full enterprise onboarding checklist (separate doc), compliance packaging.

High-level goals:
1) No long-lived seed control-plane nodes. All control plane state reconstructed from etcd snapshots + immutable etcd operator images or a managed etcd backup store.
2) Idempotent hardware-to-cluster pipeline: BMC -> iPXE -> provisioning image -> ignition -> kubeadm/k0s/k3s (experimentable) -> post-install agents.
3) Flexible Terraform modules that can produce either physical machine allocations (IPMI) or vSphere VMs from the same high-level configuration.
4) Fast recovery path: re-provisioning from golden artifact + automated etcd restore + DNS/LoadBalancer reconciliation.

Assumptions:
- Management network (VLAN) exists and has DHCP + TFTP/IPXE endpoints reachable from racks.
- vCenter has templated VM images accessible to the infra team.
- KMS for secret material is provisioned and accessible during bootstrap.
- Customer WAN/VPC connectivity handled out-of-band.

Concept: Factory pattern overview
- ‘Factory controller’ (stateless orchestration) receives a desired cluster spec and produces provisioning tasks.
- Tasks are executed by fleet agents or operator team: BMC commands for bare metal, vSphere API calls for VM creation.
- Provisioning artifact (= golden instrumented boot image) is almost identical for bare metal and VMs; behavior switches via kernel cmdline/metadata (e.g., target_role=controlplane or worker).
- After OS install, an ignition/user-data step runs a small init agent that pulls the cluster manifest + secrets and executes the Kubernetes bring-up and join steps.

Bootstrap sequence (seedless):
1) Request cluster manifest and credentials from management API.
2) Allocate nodes (Terraform modules create entries in inventory and, for vSphere, create VMs in the requested resource pool).
3) Provision NIC/BMC settings (set PXE, configure NICs, set boot order).
4) Kick nodes into network bootstrap via iPXE (chainload image served by factory TFTP/HTTP).
5) Golden image performs partitioning, writes ignition, and reboots into installed OS.
6) Init agent pulls manifest, drains puppet/chef/other pre-existing config, fetches secrets from KMS, and performs control plane install.
7) Control plane starts using an etcd operator configured to restore either from a snapshot URL in the manifest or from a bootstrap snapshot store.
8) Once API is responsive, workers join using pre-signed join tokens.
9) Post-install validation: cluster-health probes, CNI sanity checks, storage class reconciliation, node labels/taints.

Terraform module notes (patterns and pitfalls):
- module: inventory (shared between baremetal and vsphere)
  - inputs: cluster_name, node_groups (list), role, tags, hw_profile, bootstrap_metadata_url
  - outputs: host_inventory (list of {hostname, ip, bmc, mac}) -- note: output is a flattened list of strings rather than nested maps in our implementation to keep CI tooling simple.
- module: baremetal.hard-alloc
  - manages BMC creds in vault and writes ephemeral allocation records.
  - tip: keep BMC SSH/IPMI timeouts > 10s to avoid transient failures during firmware flaps.
- module: vsphere.template-provisioner
  - use customization spec to set iPXE metadata; avoid cloud-init packages that attempt to re-register hostnames with enterprise DNS.
- common issue: trying to use the same subnet for both DHCP provisioning and post-install host addressing. Separate provisioning VLANs make recovery easier.
- state considerations: lock remote Terraform state per cluster to avoid conflicting operations; we use a per-cluster S3 key and DynamoDB lock pattern in prod.

Ignition / iPXE specifics:
- chainload URL pattern: http://factory.internal/bootstrap?role={{role}}&manifest={{manifest_id}}
- golden image should mount /var/lib/factory and write a small marker file with hardware fingerprint and manifest id.
- For vSphere, ensure the OVF/Template has the same kernel+initramfs versions as bare metal golden artifact to avoid divergent behavior.

Etcd restore strategy (seedless detail):
- etccd operator checks manifest for snapshot source: s3://customer-etc-backups/cluster-abc/latest or http(s) with signed URL.
- If snapshot present, operator creates a temporary etcd cluster (3 nodes) using a sidecar restore image, seeds data, and then scales up the control plane components from 1->3 using kubeadm scale operations.
- If no snapshot found: operator bootstraps a fresh cluster and marks it ephemeral; operator triggers an alert and requires manual reconciliation (we prefer avoiding this path).

Upgrade plan notes (control plane + kubelet):
- Upgrade policy: control-plane first, then kubelet nodes in rolling window 10%. Keep older quantized images in the registry for fallbacks.
- Canary approach: provision a small ephemeral test cluster using the next kubeadm/k8s/pod-network image, run e2e smoke (curl API, schedule pods, verify PV provisioning) then roll cluster control-plane pods.
- Rollback: keep previous machine image and terraform plan for reprovisioning if kubeadm upgrade fails. For etcd failures, we revert to the snapshot used prior to the upgrade and restore cluster state on a newly provisioned control plane.

Validation checklist (post-bootstrap):
- kube-api responsive: curl /healthz and /live endpoints (200).
- etcd cluster health OK, matching expected member count.
- CNI pods Running for >= 5m.
- Storage classes present and dynamic provisioning test succeeds.
- Scheduler placing pods and tolerations working.
- Node hardware metrics emitted (IPMI sensors visible via node-exporter).

Recovery playbook (quick steps):
- If control plane fails to start: check boot artifacts, fetch ignition logs at /var/log/factory-install.log and the marker file.
- If etcd inconsistent: trigger etcd operator restore from known-good snapshot.
- If provisioning network down: isolate DHCP server and boot via local ISO to triage NIC firmware.

Operational notes and operator ergonomics:
- Make the factory orchestration idempotent: re-run operations should be no-ops when cluster already created. Use a small reconciliation loop to detect drift and emit suggested terraform plan.
- Observability: emit step events to the management plane (timestamp, node, step, status, artifact_id). Keep event payload small.
- Security: never store BMC passwords in plain text. Use Vault with lease TTLs and rotate per provisioning job.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Which kube distribution to standardize on? (kubeadm vs k0s vs upstream k8s). Initial experiments favor kubeadm for predictable upgrades, but k0s has smaller runtime.
- How do we expose a 'bootstrap-only' SSH user securely for onsite debug without leaking keys to the image? Consider one-time tokens from KMS.
- Validate performance impact of running etcd restore on same disk as live workloads — possible IO contention.

Action items (owners):
- (Ava) Build a minimal terraform module that produces a flattened inventory output for both VM and baremetal paths — due 2024-11-30.
- (Liam) Prototype etcd-operator restore flow with an S3-hosted snapshot — due 2024-12-10.
- (Priya) Test iPXE chainload with vSphere templated VMs and confirm kernel parity — due 2024-12-18.

Notes to self (voice-of-dev, quick):
- Keep golden image upgrades atomic and versioned, tag with semantic + build id.
- Write small 'health-check' binary (go) that runs pre- and post-provision checks; keep exit codes stable.
- When in doubt, prefer re-provision > live repair for consistent customer SLAs.

Appendix: Useful commands and snippets
- IPMI power cycle (example): ipmitool -I lanplus -H 10.1.2.3 -U admin -P $PASS chassis power cycle
- sample terraform inventory flatten example (pseudo): join(map("%s:%s", aws_instance.name, aws_instance.private_ip), ",")
- quick etcd snapshot restore (operator flow): "etcdctl snapshot restore /tmp/snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restored --name restored0" then point operator to restored folder.

If this pattern proves robust, we can formalize modules, add test harnesses for upgrades, and prepare a customer-facing runbook. For now — notes and experiments.

End of draft.
